name: Agra
info: Agra is a city on the Yamuna river in Uttar Pradesh, India, rebuilt in 1504–1505 by Sikandar Lodi, the capital of the Mughal emperors from Babur to Shah Jahan, and the site of the Taj Mahal and the Agra Fort.

facts.founded: An ancient city on the left bank of the Yamuna is lost in the legends of Krishna and the Mahabharata; Sikandar Lodi rebuilt Agra in 1504–1505, and Akbar founded the modern city on the right bank in 1558.
facts.where: On the banks of the Yamuna river in western Uttar Pradesh, India, about 230 kilometres south-east of Delhi, in the Braj region.
facts.known: The Lodi seat of government; the capital of the Mughal Empire; the Agra Fort; the Taj Mahal; the tombs of Akbar and Itmad-ud-daulah; Akbar's Din-i-Ilahi; the rebellion of 1857
facts.today: Agra is a city in Uttar Pradesh with a population of 1,585,704 at the 2011 census, and its Taj Mahal and Agra Fort are World Heritage Sites.

t: Sikandar Lodi rebuilt Agra in 1504–1505 and made it his seat of government, and Babur took it after defeating Ibrahim Lodi at Panipat in 1526.
Akbar built the modern city on the right bank of the Yamuna and the Agra Fort, and his grandson Shah Jahan built the Taj Mahal there from 1632.
Aurangzeb moved the court to Delhi in 1658, after which Agra passed to the Jats, the Marathas and the East India Company, and it became a district town of British India.
dyk: When Babur went to find a site for a garden at Agra, he wrote in his memoir that the country was so ugly and detestable that he crossed back over the river repulsed; he then planted gardens in every corner of the spot he had chosen.
ev: Sikandar Lodi rebuilds Agra and makes it the seat of government

sections.origins:
Agra stands on the banks of the Yamuna river in Uttar Pradesh, on a level plain about 230 kilometres south-east of Delhi, in the Braj region. Several derivations of its name have been proposed, none very satisfactory. The most accepted is the Hindi word agar, a salt pan, given because of the region's brackish soil, where salt was once made by evaporation. Others derive it from the Sanskrit agra, 'front', meaning the first of the small forests where Krishna played with the gopis of Vrindavan.

Agra has two histories. The first is that of an ancient city on the east, or left, bank of the Yamuna, which goes back so far that it is lost in the legends of Krishna and the Mahabharata. The second is that of the modern city, founded by Akbar in 1558 on the right bank. Little remains of the ancient city except a few traces of its foundations. It was a place of importance under various Hindu dynasties before the Muslim invasions of India, but its history is unclear. The 17th-century chronicler Abdullah said it was a village before the reign of Sikandar Lodi. The king of Mathura had used the Agra fort as a jail, and the site was degraded by the destruction Mahmud of Ghazni brought upon it. Masud Sa'd Salman claimed to have been there when Mahmud assaulted Agra, and said that the Raja Japal surrendered after seeing a nightmare. Mahmud nevertheless pillaged the city.
sections.growth:
Agra's period of historical importance began under Sikandar Lodi. In 1504–1505 this Afghan ruler of the Delhi Sultanate rebuilt the city and made it the seat of government. A commission he appointed inspected both sides of the Yamuna from Delhi to Etawah and chose a place on the left bank. The city grew into a large town with royal presence, officials, merchants, scholars, theologians and artists, and became one of the most important centres of Islamic learning in India.

Under the Mughals Agra was the foremost city of the subcontinent. Akbar built the modern city on the right bank, connected it with the parts of his empire and raised the ramparts of the Agra Fort, and made Agra a centre of learning, arts, commerce and religion. Before his death it had become probably one of the biggest cities in the east, with a great deal of trade in its bazaars. The English traveller Ralph Fitch, who visited in September 1585, called Agra and Fatehpur Sikri two very great cities, each much greater than London. Jahangir wrote that the city's buildings equalled several cities of Iraq, Khurasan and Transoxiana put together and that many people had built houses of three or four storeys. Jahangir loved Lahore and Kashmir more than Agra, but it remained the first city of the realm. Shah Jahan's building raised it to the pinnacle of its glory.
sections.rulers:
Sikandar Lodi, who reigned from 1489 to 1517, made Agra the seat of government of the Delhi Sultanate. After his death in 1517 the city passed to his son Ibrahim Lodi, who ruled from Agra until Babur defeated and killed him at the First Battle of Panipat in 1526. Babur sent his son Humayun ahead, and Humayun occupied the town without opposition. Babur was determined to make Agra the seat of his government. Humayun was defeated at Kanauj in 1539 by Sher Shah Suri, whose short-lived Sur Empire held the region from 1540 to 1556, until Akbar reconquered it at the Second Battle of Panipat in 1556.

Agra was the capital of the Mughal Empire under Babur, Humayun, Akbar, Jahangir and Shah Jahan, until 1658, when Aurangzeb moved the whole court to Delhi. In official correspondence Agra continued to be called the second capital of the empire. As Mughal power declined, control of the city passed in the late 18th century to the Jats, the Marathas, the Mughals again, the ruler of Gwalior and finally the East India Company. The Jats under Suraj Mal conquered it on 12 June 1761 after a month-long siege, and held it until 1774, when the Mughal commander Mirza Najaf Khan recaptured it. The Marathas took it in 1785 and the East India Company in 1803, after the Second Anglo-Maratha War. Agra was the capital of the short-lived Presidency of Agra in 1834–1836 and of the North-Western Province from 1836 to 1858.
sections.life:
Agra had a mixed population of courtiers, merchants, scholars and artists. Under Sikandar Lodi it was among the most important centres of Islamic learning in India, and under Akbar it was a centre of learning, arts, commerce and religion. Akbar founded the religion called Din-i-Ilahi, which is now extinct and which Agra is regarded as the birthplace of. The Radhaswami faith also began in Agra, and has about two million followers worldwide. The city's chronicles and travellers' accounts describe crowded lanes and bazaars: Jahangir wrote that the mass of people was so great that moving about in them was difficult, and the traveller William Finch found the city populous beyond measure.

Babur laid out the first formal Mughal garden in India, the Aram Bagh, on the bank of the Yamuna, planting roses and narcissus in beds that matched one another. Jahangir laid many gardens inside the Red Fort. Under Shah Jahan, who was known for his keen interest in architecture, craftsmen from India, Persia, the Ottoman Empire and Europe worked on the Taj Mahal, and pietra dura inlay work decorated its interiors. Marble inlay and carpets remained royal crafts of the city. After 1858 Agra was a major centre of Hindi and Urdu journalism, and the Agra Lunatic Asylum opened in 1859. Agra College, founded in 1823 by the Sanskrit scholar Pandit Gangadhar Shastri, produced the first graduate in Uttar Pradesh, and St Peter's College was founded in 1846 and St John's College in 1850.
sections.crises:
Mahmud of Ghazni assaulted Agra and pillaged it. In the later 18th century, as the Mughal empire declined, the city changed hands repeatedly. When the Jats took it on 12 June 1761 after a month-long siege, they melted the silver doors of the Taj Mahal. In 1688 the Jats under Rajaram Jat had damaged the tomb of Akbar at Sikandra to avenge his uncle Gokula Jat, who had been executed by Aurangzeb. They plundered its gold, jewels, silver and carpets, and burned Akbar's bones. Shah Jahan was confined in the Agra Fort by his son Aurangzeb from 1658 until his death in 1666.

In the rebellion of 1857 the news of the mutiny at Meerut reached Agra on 14 May. Some companies of the 44th and 67th Native Infantry mutinied on 30 May and carried the treasury they had been sent to fetch from Mathura to the rebels in Delhi, and the rest of those battalions were disarmed on 31 May. The Gwalior contingent mutinied on 15 June, and all other native units followed. On 3 July some 6,000 Europeans and associated people moved into the Agra Fort, and on 5 July a British force that attacked approaching mutineers was defeated and retreated into the fort. Despite an uprising by a mob and extreme disorder in the city, the British restored partial order by 8 July. After Delhi fell in September, a brigade under Edward Greathed reached Agra on 11 October and defeated a surprise attack, an action named the Battle of Agra. The capital of the North-Western Provinces was moved to Allahabad in 1858, and Agra declined to a provincial town.
sections.legacy:
Agra's monuments are mostly from its Mughal past. The Agra Fort, a fortress of red sandstone with a perimeter of about 2.5 kilometres, was commissioned by Akbar in 1565 and took around eight years to build, on the site of earlier fortifications by Islam Shah Suri. Jahangir and Shah Jahan changed it considerably, and Shah Jahan added marble buildings including the Moti Masjid and the Diwan-i-Khas. The Taj Mahal was built for Shah Jahan's wife Mumtaz Mahal, who died in childbirth in 1631. Its chief architect was probably the Persian Ustad Ahmad Lahori. Construction began in 1632 with upwards of twenty thousand workers, the mausoleum was finished by 1639 and the adjunct buildings by 1643, and the whole complex took 22 years. Shah Jahan's own tomb stands beside hers.

Akbar's tomb at Sikandra was completed by Jahangir in 1613, and Nur Jahan commissioned the tomb of I'timad-ud-Daulah, her father and Jahangir's chief minister, whose white marble and pietra dura presage the Taj Mahal. The Jama Masjid was built in 1648. Akbar's capital of Fatehpur Sikri, about 35 kilometres from Agra, was later abandoned. The Taj Mahal and the Agra Fort became UNESCO World Heritage Sites in 1983.

Agra is today a city of Uttar Pradesh, the fourth most populous of the state, with 1,585,704 people at the 2011 census. It has been part of Uttar Pradesh since Indian independence in 1947, and has developed into an industrial city, with leather and footwear manufacture.

summary: Agra, on the Yamuna in Uttar Pradesh, was rebuilt by Sikandar Lodi in 1504–1505 and was the capital of the Mughal emperors until Aurangzeb moved the court to Delhi in 1658. It holds the Agra Fort and the Taj Mahal, built by Shah Jahan.
references: Muḥammad Latif, Agra, Historical & Descriptive (Calcutta Central Press, 1896)
notes: Only the city's own article was available; there is no History of Agra article.
START: the article gives the ancient city no date (lost in legend). I used 1504, the year Sikandar Lodi rebuilt Agra; the modern city on the right bank is dated 1558 (Akbar).
CAPITAL MOVE: the article says Shah Jahan shifted the capital to Shahjahanabad in 1648, and also that Aurangzeb shifted the court in 1658 and that Agra was capital until 1658. I used 1658 only.

TAJ MAHAL DATES: lead says built 1632 to 1648; the Taj section says completed in 1653 in the history, mausoleum by 1639, adjunct by 1643, decoration until at least 1647, and 22 years in total. I gave 1632 start and the 1639/1643 and 22-year figures, and left the 1648 and 1653 completion dates out of the text.
Akbar built the Agra Fort: the article says the fort was commissioned in 1565 and took about eight years, and elsewhere that Akbar 'raised the ramparts'. Used as given.
Aram Bagh: history says Babur laid it out; the monuments section dates it 1528. Not dated in the text.
Sikandra: the article says Sikandar Lodi built a baradari there in 1495, before his rebuilding of Agra in 1504 and, as given, within his reign. I left it out.
Jat siege of 1761: the article says the Jats melted the silver doors of the Taj Mahal after the siege; used as given. The 1688 Jat damage to Akbar's tomb is as the article states it.
Akbar's tomb: Sikandra section says its construction began in Akbar's reign and was completed by Jahangir in 1613; the Mughal history says it was completed during Jahangir's reign. Consistent.
The Jama Masjid is described as 'attributed to' Shah Jahan's daughter Jahanara Begum, built 1648; the Mughal history says Shah Jahan built it. I gave only the date.

Population: 1,585,704 is the 2011 census figure; the article's 'roughly 1.6 million' is current-sounding, so the year is attached. The lead's 'fourth-most populous in Uttar Pradesh' is as of an unstated date.
Radhaswami Faith and Din-i-Ilahi: the article says Agra is the birthplace of both. I wrote 'regarded as' for Din-i-Ilahi only to hedge the phrasing; the article states it flatly.

Left out as tourism, rankings, transport, media, economy, pollution and the present: the Golden Triangle, visitor figures, state visits, metro, climate, sister cities, the list of notable people and the films.

Cuisine, Taj Mahotsav, later education institutions and the quotations of Tagore and Mukerji left out; the Lieutenant-Governor's death in the fort and the remark that Agra's rising was minor beside Delhi's were cut for length.
Checker flag 'Khurasan and Transoxiana' is the article's 'Trans-Oxiana' respelt.
